name: Adam Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice on an overhead crew for the city electricity company, out of the east side depot. We start at seven, load the truck, and then it's whatever the day throws at us: changing a cracked insulator, replacing a rotten pole, hanging new service drops to houses. I'm still the one sent up for the simple jobs while Gary, my foreman, watches from the ground and tells me what I did wrong. I love being up a pole on a clear morning, honestly, but the paperwork at the end of the day wears me out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They gave every crew a tablet last year for work orders and photos. I hate it. I'd rather write it in my notebook, and Dev, the other apprentice, ends up filling mine in while I eat my sandwich. I'm not proud of that, but it's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. The tablet was meant to change everything and it mostly made Gary swear more. At the union meeting I'd say, good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter, like staffing on storm nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on. I finish my apprenticeship in two years, I get my journeyman ticket, the pay goes up properly. My partner Lena is a nurse, her job isn't going anywhere, and we've got about three months of bills put away. That's not rich, but it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing much changes. I keep turning up, keep studying for the second-year exams, and keep putting a bit away each month. I'd go to the union meetings like I already do, because the fight over crew sizes is there with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. I didn't sign up for this trade to be a computer person. I signed up because my uncle did it and I liked the idea of fixing things people can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the paperwork wears you out. If AI did take some of that routine stuff, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. If it fills in the work order for me, fine, but I won't go looking for it. I'll let Dev press the buttons and I'll hold the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena spend on if things just stayed steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving for a deposit on a small flat. Rent went up again in March, that's the one thing that bugs me. If AI changes nothing, the landlord is still the problem, not the robots.

say: I'd tell the union meeting the **AI hype** fizzled, so let's talk about **storm staffing** instead.
I'd joke that the tablet only made my **foreman swear** more.
think: Privately I think my **apprenticeship** carries on and I get my journeyman ticket in two years.
Lena's **nursing job** and our three months of savings make me feel fairly safe.
do: Keep studying for the **second-year exams** and turning up at seven every day.
Keep going to **union meetings** about crew sizes on storm nights.
Keep putting a little into the **flat deposit** each month despite the March rent rise.
feel: **Relieved**, because he never wanted his trade to become computer work.
A little **irritated** that rent, not AI, is still his real money problem.
S0.quote: If AI changes nothing, the landlord is still the problem, not the robots.
fieldNote: He openly lets another apprentice do his **tablet work**, and says so without much shame.
His real money worry is **rent**, not technology; the rise in March came up unprompted.
**Union meetings** are part of his normal week, not a reaction to AI.

steps.text: Finish the second-year apprenticeship exams on the east side crew
Keep paying into the flat deposit fund with Lena each month
Go to the monthly union meeting about storm-night crew sizes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office lot are getting hammered and we should stand with them. The dispatchers and the planners at our depot do a lot of exactly that stuff, checking, booking, planning. At work I'd tell people we should back them, because once the bosses get away with it upstairs they'll try it on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think I'm mostly fine for a while. Nobody's building a robot that climbs a wet pole in a gale next year. But I'd hate the job more, because everything would come through that tablet, the job list, the checks, the sign-off, and I'm bad with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal in writing that no lineworker loses their job over the new software. I'd ask Dev to sit with me one evening and show me the new screens properly, because I'd have no choice. Money-wise, I'd keep saving the same, maybe a bit more, in case overtime gets cut when the planning gets automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like when they changed the shift pattern two years back. Nothing terrible happened, but everyone was on edge for months and Gary snapped at everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen in dispatch. She's been taking our calls for twenty years and she knows every street by heart. If a computer starts sending us out, she's the one who goes, and I'd be gutted, she brings cake on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit with Dev and learn the screens. Isn't that learning AI, which you said you wouldn't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd learn the bit they make me learn and not one button more. That's not me changing, that's me keeping my job.

say: I'd say we should **stand with dispatch** and planners, because the bosses will come for **line crews** next.
I'd tell the crew no lineworker should lose a job over **new software**.
think: I think my **hands-on job** is safe for now, because no robot climbs a wet pole next year.
I'd hate the job more, because the **job list** and sign-off would all go through the tablet.
do: Push the union for a **written promise** that new software costs no lineworker jobs.
Sit with Dev one evening to learn the **new screens**, and nothing more.
Save a bit more in case **overtime** shrinks when planning is automated.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the months after the shift pattern changed and everyone was on edge.
**Gutted** for older office staff like Maureen in dispatch.
S1.quote: I'd learn the bit they make me learn and not one button more. Learning the new screens isn't me changing, it's me keeping my job.
fieldNote: He thinks of the **office staff** first, which fits his union loyalties.
When pushed, he admits he'd **learn the screens**, but frames it as survival, not change.
His own work feels safe, so the mood is about **tension at the depot** rather than his pay.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a no-job-losses deal on the new software
Spend one evening with Dev learning the new tablet screens
Put an extra bit aside in case storm overtime drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry and I'd say it loud. I'd say the companies built this to get rid of people and the government let them. Online I'd share every petition going, and at work I'd say we need the union out in force before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. Two years for the thinking stuff, so all the office people are gone by 2028, and then robots by 2031. I'd be thirty-one. I'll have just got my ticket, just started earning properly, and the thing I trained for would be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd do what I know, which is finish my apprenticeship as fast as I can, because a journeyman gets kept longer than an apprentice. I'd go to every union meeting and probably get on the committee, which I've never wanted to do. I'd save hard, cut the takeaways and the football tickets, and try to get to six months of bills before the robots show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. I'm not someone who changes easily, I know that about myself. Lena's the one who adapts, I just dig in, and I don't think digging in works here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap matters, sort of. In those three years the dispatch, the planning, the work orders all go to the computer, so we'd be taking our jobs off a screen with no Maureen to ring. Then the robots come, and the only thing left for people might be checking the robots, which needs exactly the tablet skills I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might have to live on her wage for a while. She'd say that's fine, and I'd hate that it's fine. My dad never once lived on my mum's wage, and I know that's old-fashioned of me.

say: I'd say **companies built this** to get rid of workers and the **government** let them.
I'd share every **petition** and tell the crew the union needs to act now.
think: Privately I'm **scared**, because robots arrive around **2031**, when I'm thirty-one and just qualified.
I fear the only human work left is **checking robots**, which needs the tablet skills I lack.
do: Finish the **apprenticeship** as fast as possible, since journeymen get kept longer.
Join the **union committee**, which he has never wanted to do.
Cut takeaways and football tickets to reach **six months** of savings by 2031.
feel: Like the **floor is tilting** under him.
**Ashamed** at the thought of living on Lena's wage, while knowing that feeling is old-fashioned.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner we might have to live on her nurse's wage for a while. She'd say that's fine, and I'd hate that it's fine.
fieldNote: He knows he **digs in** rather than adapts, and says it plainly.
He sees the three-year gap as losing **dispatch** first, then his own hands-on work.
His **pride** about earning shows through his progressive talk.

steps.text: Stand for the union branch committee at the east side depot
Drop the football season ticket and weekly takeaways
Build savings to six months of bills before 2031
Sign and share petitions for limits on replacing workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Like the last one, but with more time. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said with the fast one, but calmer. Five years means we can actually organise, so I'd be telling people to get the union to bargain for retraining money and a slow rollout. I'd say it at the pub too, which my mates would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years plus three for the robots is 2034. I'd be thirty-five, journeyman for six years. That's long enough to save something, but it's still my whole working life cut in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket, then push to get onto the storm restoration team, because robots will struggle longest with storm damage. I'd keep the savings going and put a bit into the union strike fund. I wouldn't retrain into something else, I'd just try to be the last kind of lineworker they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. I'd still lie awake some nights, just not every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why storm work in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every storm is different. Last February we had a tree through three spans on Mill Road and a pole snapped at the base, and nobody could have planned that from a screen. A robot built for normal days won't know what to do with that mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start doing now, in 2026, if you knew this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start asking Gary to teach me the storm stuff properly instead of just sending me up for the easy jobs. And I'd stop letting Dev do my tablet work, because I'd need to know it.

say: I'd say five years gives the **union** time to bargain for **retraining money** and a slow rollout.
I'd make the same case at the **pub**, even if my mates got bored.
think: I'd be thirty-five when **robots arrive** in 2034, so my working life gets **cut in half**.
Six years as a journeyman is enough to **save something**, but not to feel safe.
do: Ask Gary now to teach him **storm work** properly, not just the easy jobs.
Move onto the **storm restoration** team once he has his journeyman ticket.
Put money into the **union strike fund** while keeping his savings going.
feel: He'd still **lie awake** some nights, just not every night.
S3.quote: Last February a tree came through three spans on Mill Road. Nobody could have planned that storm damage from a screen, and no robot built for normal days will either.
fieldNote: He bets on **storm work** as the last job robots can do, using a real Mill Road job as proof.
With more time, he'd finally stop handing his **tablet work** to Dev.
He still won't consider **leaving the trade**; he wants to be the last kind of lineworker needed.

steps.text: Ask Gary to teach him storm restoration jobs this winter
Pay into the union strike fund every month
Keep the flat savings growing towards six months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say ten years is ages and people panic too much. That's what everyone at the depot would say, so I'd say it too. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't post much anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, ten years and then robots in 2039 means I'd be forty. Forty is a bad age to lose a trade. Too old to start fresh easily, too young to stop, and Lena and I might have kids by then, which changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first years I'd do nothing different, if I'm honest, which I know is the wrong answer. Maybe around 2033 or so I'd start saving harder and asking the union what the plan is. I'd think about whether I should do an evening course in something, but I'd probably put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slow sort of worry. Not loud, more like a damp patch you know you should look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd likely put off the evening course. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot up a pole with my own eyes. Until I see it, I don't believe it, that's how I am. My uncle laughed at the bucket trucks once too, and then he used one for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did have kids by then, what would change in how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a lot more scared. Losing my job at thirty-five with no kids is one thing. Losing it at forty with a baby is the kind of thing that makes a man say yes to any rubbish job.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages and people **panic too much**, like everyone at the depot.
I'd stay **quiet online**, as I usually do.
think: Losing my trade at **forty**, when robots arrive in 2039, would be the worst possible age.
If Lena and I have **kids** by then, the stakes get much higher.
do: Carry on as normal for the **first few years**, while admitting that's probably wrong.
Start **saving harder** around 2033 and ask the union what its plan is.
Think about an **evening course**, though he expects to keep putting it off.
feel: A **slow worry**, like a damp patch he knows he should look at.
S4.quote: I won't believe it until I see a robot up a pole with my own eyes. My uncle laughed at bucket trucks once, then used one for thirty years.
fieldNote: He knows that **doing nothing** is the wrong answer and says so himself.
Only **seeing a robot** with his own eyes would move him to act.
The idea of **children by 2039** makes the long wait feel heavier, not lighter.

steps.text: Wait until robots are seen on real poles before any course
Start saving harder from around 2033 for a possible gap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It lands right when I've just got my ticket, and I'm not someone who switches easily. What would help is the union having a proper deal ready, with retraining paid for by the company and not just a leaflet, and a law that says they can't sack a whole crew at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Lena. She'd be fine in all five, and part of me is glad, and part of me is ashamed that I'd be leaning on her. I think a lot of blokes my age feel that and don't say it.

headlineQuote: I'm not someone who changes easily, I know that about myself. Lena's the one who adapts, I just dig in, and I don't think digging in works here.
portrait: Adam is a **second-year apprentice** on an overhead line crew in the city, living with Lena, a nurse.
He loves climbing but **avoids the tablet** and lets a fellow apprentice do his work orders.
He leans on the **union** and blames companies and government for replacing workers.
He stays calm if AI stalls, but the **fast AGI picture** hits right as he qualifies.
He admits he **digs in** instead of adapting, and would only act once he sees robots himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive just after he gets his journeyman ticket.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** with company-paid retraining, not just a leaflet.
A **law** stopping firms from sacking whole crews at once.
